questions.q: Why is character-level tokenization the recommended default for this capstone's tiny model?
options: It produces the shortest possible token sequences
It keeps the vocabulary small, which keeps the embedding table and output layer small, at the cost of longer sequences
It is the only tokenization scheme PyTorch supports
It removes the need for a validation split
questions.explain: Character-level vocabularies are tiny (around 65 characters for Tiny Shakespeare), which keeps the embedding table and final projection layer small — important for a model with only a few million parameters. The tradeoff is longer token sequences than word or BPE-level tokenization.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff of moving from character-level to word-level or BPE tokenization for this project?
options: Word/BPE tokenization is always slower to decode
Word/BPE tokenization cannot be used with a decoder-only transformer
Word/BPE tokenization shortens sequences but grows the vocabulary, increasing embedding and output-layer size
There is no real tradeoff; word-level is strictly better
questions.explain: Word-level or BPE vocabularies run into the thousands or tens of thousands of tokens, which meaningfully increases parameter count in the embedding table and output projection — real cost for a small model, even though sequences get shorter.

questions.q: Which dataset does this lesson recommend as the standard starting point for a from-scratch tiny language model?
options: The full English Wikipedia dump
A proprietary licensed news corpus
Tiny Shakespeare, a roughly 1.1-million-character plain-text corpus
A dataset of copyrighted song lyrics
questions.explain: Tiny Shakespeare is small, clean, single-file, and has enough internal structure for a tiny model to visibly learn from — making it the standard first dataset for from-scratch language model training.

questions.q: What is a realistic parameter-count target for the model you'll build in this capstone?
options: 100,000 or fewer parameters
Roughly 1-5 million parameters
At least 1 billion parameters
Exactly the same size as GPT-2
questions.explain: A model with 4-6 transformer blocks, 4-8 heads, and 128-256 embedding dimensions lands around 1-5 million parameters — small enough to train quickly on a single GPU (or more slowly on CPU) while still learning visible structure.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should you decide before writing any training code?
options: The exact wording of the model card
What 'done' looks like: stable loss behavior, locally coherent generation, and a reportable perplexity
Which cloud provider to deploy the model to
The exact learning rate to the fourth decimal place
questions.explain: The lesson asks you to define your finish line up front — training loss falling with validation loss stabilizing, locally coherent generated text, and a perplexity number you can explain — rather than training first and deciding what counts as success afterward.
